i
QUESTION PRESENTED
Florida has long used six -person juries to try
non-capital offenses.  In Williams v. Florida , 399
U.S. 78 (1970), this Court upheld that practice as
consistent with the Sixth Amendment.  After carefully examining text and history , this Court concluded that nothing in the Sixth Amendment clearly
required 12-person criminal juries .  Instead, a
smaller jury fulfills the constitutional guarantee
when it remains an “interposition between the accused and his accuser of the commonsense judgment
of a group of laymen, and . . . the community participation and shared responsibility that results from
that group ’s determination of guilt or innocence .”
Id. at 100.  For 56 years, Florida and other states
have relied on Williams, convicting countless defendants using that procedure and building courtrooms tailored for  six-person juries.  Presently,
5,200 criminal direct appeals await resolution  in
Florida; many concern convictions rendered by sixperson juries.
Petitioner’s is one such case.  Florida suspended
his chiropractor license after multiple female patients reported he was sexually abusing them.  Undeterred, Petitioner continued to practice chiropractic medicine—a felony under Florida law.  A six-person jury unanimously convicted him of five counts.
The question presented is:
Whether the Court should overrule Williams and
hold that the Sixth and Fourteenth Amendments require the use of 12-person juries.

ii

were the only parties to the proceeding in the court
whose judgment is under review.

1
INTRODUCTION
Six Floridians unanimously convicted  Petitioner
Hamed Kian of numerous felony offenses.  That judgment complied with the Constitution.  In Williams v.
Florida, this Court held , 7-1, that the Sixth Amendment permits Florida’s use of six -person juries.  399
U.S. 78, 102–03 (1970).
Williams began with constitutional text and history.  After r eviewing the same evidence Petitioner
presents here, the Court found that any rule making
“12” an essential feature of the jury right “would require considerably more evidence than we have been
able to discover in the history and language of the
Constitution.”  Id.  Then, concluding that neither text
nor history supported a 12 -person requirement,  the
Court examined the jury right’s “purposes.”  It held
that six-person juries afford defendants the full protection of the jury: “the interposition between the accused and his accuser of the commonsense judgment
of a group of laymen.” Id. at 100.
Williams has aged well.  To be sure, history shows
that the default common-law jury size was 12 in 1791.
But it equally reflects that jury size varied over the
centuries in England and America.  Indeed, the very
sources Petitioner touts acknowledged that jury size
was legislatively modifiable.  And 12 jurors are plainly
unnecessary to satisfy a jury’s core function: “to prevent oppression by the Government ” by “safeguard[ing] against the corrupt or overzealous prosecutor and against the compliant, biased, or eccentric
judge.”  Id.  Six-person juries fulfill that constitutional
guarantee just as effectively as 12-person juries.

2
In any event , stare decisis  forecloses Petitioner’s
arguments.  Williams, a near-unanimous decision, differs starkly from Apodaca, the fractured and confused
case this Court overruled in Ramos.  Massive reliance
interests rest on Williams’ shoulders.  More than half
of the states use smaller juries for at least some nonpetty offenses.  So overruling Williams would imperil
many thousands of criminal convictions nationwide—
dramatically more than those implicated by Ramos.
Overruling Williams would almost certainly require
overruling Colegrove, where this Court blessed
smaller-than-12 civil juries.  And overturning Williams solely because it reached a  different originalist
answer than the Court might prefer today would declare open season on  this Court’s criminal jurisprudence.  If Williams falls, no principled rationale could
sustain the exclusionary rule, Miranda, and modern
Eighth Amendment jurisprudence.
The Court should affirm.
STATEMENT OF THE CASE
A. Legal background
Responding to concerns that the jury system was
consuming one third of its budget, Florida amended
its Constitution in 1875 to permit the legislature to
reduce the size of juries.  The measure received overwhelming support from Florida’s Reconstruction legislature, including numerous black legislators.  In
1877, the legislature set the jury size for all non-capital crimes at six.  Infra II.C.2.
Williams resolved a constitutional challenge to
Florida’s 6-person juries.  In a nearly unanimous decision, the Court held that Florida’s six -person juries

3
did not violate the Sixth Amendment, as incorporated
by the Fourteenth Amendment.  399 U.S. at 103.
B. Factual and procedural background
Petitioner was a Flori da-licensed chiropractor .
During his practice, Petitioner touched a female patient’s genitals and labia  multiple times against her
will, placed his face near her genitals, and attempted
to kiss her on the lips afterwards.  State’s Mot. to Take
Judicial Notice, 4 n.1., State of Florida v. Hamed Kian,
2022-CF-002973AMB (Fla. Cir. Ct.) .  After that patient filed an administrative complaint, Florida’s
Board of Chiropractic Medicine permanently prohibited Petitioner from treating female patients without
a licensed and Board-approved female chaperone and
monitor.  Id.
Petitioner ignored this prohibition.  He treated a
female patient alone four times.  Id. at 7–10.  Without
his patient’s consent, Petitioner touched or rubbed her
genital area for at least 15 minutes.  Id. at 9.  He later
came to the patient’s apartment with massage oil and
asked her to remove her pants.  Id. at 10.  When the
patient expressed reluctance, Petitioner told her, “[o]h
now we are being modest, I have seen you naked.”  Id.
Learning this, Florida’s Surgeon General immediately
suspended Petitioner’s license, finding his practice to
be “an immediate, serious danger to the health, safety,
or welfare of the public.” Id. at 15.
Petitioner nevertheless resumed practicing
months later.  In response, prosecutors charged him
with five counts of practicing chiropractic medicine
with a suspended license, a third-degree felony.  Fla.
Stat. § 460.411(1)(b); Pet. App. 3.

4
Petitioner’s non-capital charges entitled him to a
six-person jury.  See Fla. Const. art. I, § 22 (“The right
of trial by jury shall be secure to all and remain inviolate.  The qualifications and the number of jurors, not
fewer than six, shall be fixed by law.”); Fla. Stat.
§ 913.10 (“Twelve persons shall constitute a jury to try
all capital cases, and six persons shall constitute a
jury to try all other criminal cases.”).  That jury unanimously convicted Petitioner of all five counts.  He was
sentenced to 366 days in prison, followed by 10 years’
probation.  Pet. App. 3.
Petitioner appealed to Florida’s Fourth District
Court of Appeal , arguing that a six -person jury violated his constitutional rights under the Sixth  and
Fourteenth Amendments.  The Fourth District affirmed without a written opinion.  Pet. App. 2 .  This
Court granted certiorari.
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
Williams was correct.  The Sixth Amendment does
not require that juries always consist of twelve members.  Its text makes no mention of 12.  And the historical evidence isn’t as simple as Petitioner suggests.
Jury size has varied significantly over the centuries .
Even where the default size was 12, it was always subject to legislative modification.  And the jury’s core
purpose—interposing a body of laymen between the
state and individual—doesn’t turn on a 12-juror composition.  Nor is jury size the only common-law incident that’s experienced substantial modification.  Indeed, constitutionalizing all incidents of the 1791 common-law jury would make juries unrecognizable .
Only middle-class property owners could serve as jurors, and voir dire would be eliminated.  Judges could

5
coach jurors to desired results and starve them into
unanimity.  J uries could decide for themselves what
the law was.  Plea bargains would be history.
Williams was right, but even if not , stare decisis
should save it.    The well-worn stare decisis factors all
favor Williams’ retention.  First, Williams’ reversal
would force states to re -try thousands of cases on direct appeal, further straining already-rangy budgets.
So too with the federal government in cases where 11
jurors return verdicts .  Victims will relive trauma
when called to re-testify.  Sadly, prosectors facing reopened convictions will clear the onrush by simply dismissing charges or offering sweetheart plea deals.
Federal c ivil six-person juries won’t e scape either —
Federal Civil Rule 48(a) was predicated on Williams’
reasoning.
Second, Williams was well reasoned and originalist, even if the Court would reach a different result
today.  Third, Williams and Ballew v. Georgia , 435
U.S. 223 (1978),  create a workable doctrine : Juries
must have at least six  jurors, a brightline rule upon
which at least 27 states have relied.  Fourth, Williams
is consistent with other cases, including Ramos.  Nonunanimity alters how a jury functions; a jury size of
six does not.  Fifth, no empirical data clearly demonstrates that six -person juries disadvantage defendants or are inferior to 12-person juries.
And if Williams must fall as insufficiently originalist, so must Strickland, Gideon, Zerbst, Weeks, Mapp,
Miranda, and the lion ’s share of this Court’s Eighth
Amendment jurisprudence, which made no originalist
pretensions at all.  Finally, Florida’s six-person juries

6
have no  racially discriminatory origins, unlike the
non-unanimity rule this Court forbade in Ramos.
ARGUMENT
I. Williams correctly held that  the Sixth
Amendment does not compel the use of 12 -
person juries.
In Williams v. Florida , this Court held that the
Sixth Amendment does not mandate the use of 12-person juries.  399 U.S. at 102–03.  Even setting aside
stare decisis , Petitioner fails to show that Williams
erred.  The Sixth Amendment derives its meaning
from text and history .  See Ramos v. Louisiana , 590
U.S. 83, 89–93 (2020).  Its text, however, nowhere says
that juries must consist of 12 members.   It doesn’t
speak to jury size at all.  To prevail, Petitioner must
therefore show that  the Founding public would have
understood any jury with fewer than 12 members to
be no jury at all—that the number 12 was an implicit
and essential ingredient in the term “trial by . . . jury.”
He cannot.
A. The Sixth Amendment does not speak to
jury size.
“Constitutional analysis must begin with the language of the instrument, which offers a fixed standard
for ascertaining what our founding document means.”
Dobbs v. Whole Women ’s Health Org. , 597 U.S. 215,
235 (2022) (cleaned up).  When the Constitution’s text
“makes no express reference” to a particular right, the
claimant “must show that the right is somehow implicit in the constitutional text.”  Id.

7
The right to trial by jury in criminal cases appears
twice in the Constitution.  First, Article III states that
“[t]he trial of all crimes, except in cases of impeachment, shall be by jury.”  U.S. Const. art. III, § 2, cl. 3.
“[S]uch trial,” Article III specifies, “shall be held in the
state where the said crimes shall have been committed; but when not committed within any state, the
trial shall be at such place or places as the Congress
may by law have directed.”  Id.
Second, the Sixth Amendment  provides that “[i]n
all criminal prosecutions, the accused shall enjoy the
right to a speedy and public trial, by an impartial jury
of the State and district wherein the crime shall have
been committed, which district shall have been previously ascertained by law[.]”  U.S. Const. amend. VI.
Petitioner declares it “unmistakable” that “the
phrase ‘trial by an impartial jury’ referred to a 12-person jury at the time the Sixth Amendment was enacted.”  Pet. Br. 18–19.  Incorrect.
Starting at the beginning, the Sixth Amendment’s
text doesn’t dictate jury size.  It certainly could have.
The Framers carefully specified  some features they
believed indispensable : Juries shall be “impartial,”
and “of the State and district wherein the crime shall
have been committed, which district shall have been
previously ascertained by law[.]”  U.S. Const. amend.
VI.
Notably absent is any requirement that a jury consist of 12 jurors.  Yet the Framers hardly shied away
from numerical specificity elsewhere in the Constitution.  They provided for “two Senators” from each
state, elected to terms of “ six Years,” U.S. Const. art.

8
I, § 3, cl. 1, authorized amendment of the Constitution
when proposed by “two-third[s]” of Congress and ratified by “three -fourths” of the states , id. art. V , required that impeachment convictions be obtained by
vote of “two thirds” of the Senate, id. art. I, § 3, cl. 6,
limited the President to terms of “4 Years,” id. art. II,
§ 1, cl. 2 , and vested the judicial power in “one supreme court.”  Id. art. III, §  1.  When numbers mattered, the Framers wrote them down.
If, as Petitioner suggests, the Founding generation
believed “jury” meant only a 12-person jury, the Framers could have easily specified it.  They didn’t.  See
Williams, 399 U.S. at 96 –97 (“[W]here Congress
wanted to leave no doubt that it was incorporating existing common -law features of the jury system, it
knew how to use express language to that effect.”).
Because the Sixth Amendment’s text doesn’t dictate jury size, legislatures may determine it unless Petitioner can show that “trial by an impartial jury,” in
its historical context,  was necessarily understood to
convey a right to 12 jurors.  To be sure, constitutional
language may bear extra-textual implications, but
this requires strong evidence.   See United States v.
Rahimi, 602 U.S. 680, 715 (2024) (Kavanaugh, J., concurring) (“As a general matter, the text of the Constitution says what it means and means what it says.”) .
In Ramos, this Court explained that the term “trial by
an impartial jury” “surely meant something,” and consulted the “common law,” “state practices in the
founding era,” and contemporaneous “ opinions and
treatises” to discern what that “something” was.  590

9
U.S. at 89–90.  It concluded that the evidence for constitutionalizing unanimous jury verdicts was “unmistakable.”  Id. at 90.
  Petitioner hasn’t made that showing here.
B. 12-person juries were not so essential to
the 18th century notion of a “jury” as to be
impliedly codified in the Sixth Amendment.
No one disputes that the default jury size at common law was 12.  That, however, isn’t the question.
As Williams recognized, the correct inquiry asks
“whether the constitutional guarantee of a trial by
‘jury’ necessarily requires trial by exactly 12 persons.”
399 U.S. at 86 (emphasis added).  The answer to that
question is no.
First, jury size has fluctuated over time and was
always understood to be legislatively modifiable.  Several prominent Framers took that view.  Second, Williams correctly determined that the jury right’s essential elements were those central to the right’s purpose—the interposition of a deliberative body of one’s
peers to decide guilt or innocence.  Juries of 12 aren’t
essential to the achievement of that objective.  Third,
the idea that every feature of the 1791 common-law
jury was constitutionalized is unserious; this Court
would never reinstate well-established common -law
practices like starving juries until they rendered verdicts or barring defendants from waiving the right to
jury trials.

10
1. Historically, j ury size varied and was
subject to legislative modification.
Jury size varied over the centuries, and history illustrates that, unlike juror unanimity, it was not understood to be an essential element of trial by jury and
thus was subject to legislative modification.
Early developments .  The jury’s predecessors
lacked any solicitude for 12 members.  The first bodies
that looked like juries —inquests in Scandinavia and
the Carolingian Empire —gathered information  for
fiscal and administrative purposes .  John Baker, An
Introduction to English Legal History  79 (5th ed.
2019).  They varied widely in size.  Frankish inquests
could consist of “66, 41, 20, 17, 13, 11, 8, 7, 53, 15, and
a great variety of other numbers.”  Williams, 399 U.S.
at 87 n.19 (quoting James B. Thayer, The Jury and Its
Development, 5 Harv . L. Rev. 295 (1892)).  A nd Norman inquests “show all sorts of numbers —4, 5, 6, 12,
13—18, 21, 27, 30, and so on.”  Id. (same).
Early juries consisted of less than 12 as well .  Juries were initially used as adjudicative bodies around
1220.  Baker, supra, at 80.  The first treatise on English law, Glanvill, refers to a jury of eight to determine
the defense of infancy in land disputes.  The treatise
on the laws and customs of the realm of England commonly called Glanvill  159–160 (G. D. G. Hall trans.,
1965).  Such land disputes birthed the common law
itself.  W.L. Warren, Henry II, 337–341 (1973).1  Cases
recorded in Bracton’s Note Book between 1217 and

1219 refer to juries of 9, 36, and 40.  Thayer, supra, at
295.
Around the 1 4th century, 12 became the default
size of the English common-law petit jury—at least in
most types of trials.  Williams, 399 U.S. at 87 n.19 (citing Austin Scott, Fundamentals of Procedure in Actions at Law 75–76 (1922)).   Yet that number appears
to have been arbitrary—not some deliberate decision
tied to the jury’s function.  Patrick Devlin, Trial by
Jury 8 (1956).  Many have guessed at 12’s significance.
Edward Coke speculated that English law “delighteth
herselfe in the number of 12” because there are “12
judges of ancient time for tryall of matters of law in
the Exchequer Chamber.”  1 Edward Coke, The First
Part of the Institutes of the Laws of England  155.a.
155.b. (Charles Butler ed., 18th ed. 1823).   “[I]n ancient time,” Coke added, there were “twelve Counsellors of State,” and “the number of twelve is much respected in holy writ, as 12 apostles, 12 stones, 12
tribes, &c.”  Id.  Blackstone surmised that it may have
come from Greece’s 12 pagan deities, or from Norway
via the Norman Conquest.  3 William Blackstone,
Commentaries on the Laws of England 365 n.i. (1768).
These interesting theories make one thing clear: The
number 12 was more “historical accident” than fixed
principle.  Williams, 399 U.S. at 89.
English common law.  The 12-person jury wasn’t
inevitable at common law, either.  In 1631, in Tredymmock v. Perryman, famed lawyer Sir Henry Rolle argued that the use of six jurors in a Cornwall debt judgment was not erroneous as “ secundum confetudinem
ibidem a tempore , &c”  (custom since time immemorial).  3 George Croke, Reports of Sir George Croke

12
259–60 (Thomas Leach ed., 4th ed. 1793).  Rolle
thought that “the trial then by the custom may be by
six,” and cited the “multitude of records in twenty several courts in Cornwall where trials may be by six, by
customs there used.”  Id.
The King’s Bench disagreed, holding that “such a
custom is void, and against the common law.”  Id.  But
the court acknowledged an important principle: Parliament could alter j ury size.  Id.  The King’s Bench
observed that Wales had trials by six through an act
of Parliament.  Id.2  The question for Cornwall, therefore, was whether six-person juries “had been so provided for by parliament.”  Id.
For particular areas of law,  moreover, 12-person
juries only became the rule  after the 18 th century.
For “ [i]nquests of [o]ffice”—used to adjudicate the
“Writ of Waste” —“less than Twelve may serve .”

A. Stare decisis serves critical interests  and
applies in this case.
Stare decisis  cautions against overruling precedent merely because the Court “would decide a case
differently now than [it] did then. ”  Kimble v. Marvel
Entm’t, LLC, 576 U.S. 446, 455 (2015).  It is the “preferred course” because it “promotes the evenhanded,
predictable, and consistent development of legal principles, fosters reliance on judicial decisions, and contributes to the actual and perceived integrity of the
judicial process.”  Payne v. Tennessee , 501 U.S. 808,
827 (1991) ; see also Ramos, 590 U.S. at 116  (Kavanaugh, J., concurring in part ).  “[A]ny departure ”
from stare decisis “demands special justification.”  Arizona v. Rumsey, 467 U.S. 203, 212 (1984).
Several factors guide the stare decisis  analysis.
The Court “has traditionally considered ‘the quality of
the decision’s reasoning; its consistency with related
decisions; legal developments since the decision; and
reliance on the decision.’”  Ramos, 590 U.S. at 106
(quoting Franchise Tax Bd. of Cal. v. Hyatt, 587 U.S.
230, 232 (2019)).   Also relevant is w hether a precedent’s rule has proved “unworkable.”  Payne, 501 U.S.
at 827.
Petitioner would circumvent that test  altogether.
Stare decisis is inapplicable, he says, because “Ramos
[e]ffectively [o]verruled Williams.”  Pet. Br. 24.  As Petitioner sees it, Ramos “‘repudiated the reasoning on
which’ the Court relied in Williams,” robbing Williams
of “any ongoing ‘vitality.’”  Pet. Br. 24, 26.  True, Ramos instructs courts to view the Sixth Amendment

that crime—like an early American—would “surely be
put to death.”  4 Blackstone, supra, at 194.
And of course,  there’s Miranda v. Arizona .  384
U.S. 436 (1966).   Miranda is plainly “at odds with
American and English legal history.”  Id. at 531
(White, J., dissenting).  “At common law, there was no
requirement that a suspect be advised in pre -trial interrogation that he could remain silent or that his
statements could be used against him.”  Dep’t of Just.,
Report to the Attorney General on the Law of Pre-Trial
Interrogation (Feb. 12, 1986), https://perma.cc/6MXS-
BABT; see also Wilson v. United States, 162 U.S. 613,
623–24 (1896).  Instead, common-law courts excluded
confessions if they were involuntary under all the circumstances.  E.g., Sparf v. United States, 156 U.S. 51,
54–56 (1895).  Receipt of a police warning was proof
that the suspect’s confession was voluntary, but was
never required.  Gerald M. Caplan, Questioning Miranda, 38 Vand. L. Rev. 1417, 1423 (1985).
Williams doesn’t resemble these cases from the
make-it-up-as-you-go canon.  It considered text, history, and tradition.  If this Court overturns Williams

49
as insufficiently originalist, what principled justification would allow it to leave these anti-originalist cases
intact?
2. Ramos didn’t implicate the same slippery slope.
Four Justices didn’t even believe “Apodaca supplie[d]
a governing precedent,” rendering stare decisis inapt.
Ramos, 590 U.S. at 101 (plurality op.); see also id. at

And the deciding votes in Ramos came from two

had to bend.   Id. at 111–12, 114 –15 (Sotomayor, J.,

J., concurring) (“[T]he origins and effects of the non -
unanimous jury rule strongly support overruling Apodaca.”).
The history of Florida’s six-person juries reveals no
such discriminatory origins.  The legislative alteration
was motivated by cost savings, not racism.25  In 1874,

Journal 42–43 (the “expense of jurors and witnesses
equals one-third of the whole cost of the State government, excluding that of sessions of the Legislature” ).
Soon after, the legislature proposed a constitutional
amendment allowing it to reduce jury sizes.  That proposal received overwhelming, bipartisan support—including from black legislators.  It was drafted by a
joint committee of eight, which included two black legislators: John Wallace and Frederick Hill.  See 1874
House Journal 130; Canter Brown Jr., Florida’s Black
Public Officials, 1867-1924 134–35, 146 (1998).  Then,
in 1875, Florida’s House of Representatives approved
the measure unanimously, with 10 black legislators in
support.  1875 House Journal 119.  The Senate vote
was similarly unanimous.  1875 Senate Journal 159.
Four of those senators were black.  In 1877, the legislature passed legislation that reduced the size of noncapital juries to six.  See 1877 House Journal 187–88;
1877 Senate Journal 208.
Petitioner insinuates otherwise.  See Pet. Br. 36–
37.  Yet he cites no direct evidence that Florida’s jury
size reduction was motivated by a post-Reconstruction
conspiracy to keep blacks of f juries or deprive racial
minorities of their jury trial  rights.  See id.; cf. Br. of
Fla. Assoc. Crim. Defense Lawyers 4 (“Amicus has not
located a letter, journal entry, or floor speech in which
a Florida legislator said that reducing the jury size to
six was done to preserve white supremacy.”).  His best
evidence is that other states employed other methods
of disenfranchising black jurors, like allowing non -

unanimous verdicts.  But no one would argue that all

anyway.  His crimes don’t impugn the entire profession.  And not every post-Reconstruction government
action is inherently tarnished with racist motivations.
Petitioner casts further discriminatory aspersions
by suggesting that the 1877 law “reinstated an ‘integrity, fair character, sound judgment and intelligence’
test for jurors .”  Pet. Br. 12; see also id. at 37.  But
Florida introduced that requirement in 1868, while
under federal supervision and occupied by federal

Far from racist, the 1877 legislation added the sensible requirement that potential jurors must not have
“formed or expressed an opinion.”  The Acts and Resolutions Adopted by the Legislature of Florida at its
Ninth Session 52–53 (1877).  Add to all that, Florida
in 1873 criminalized discrimination against jurors “by
